# Day 10: CNNs, Classic & Modern

## Learning goals

By the end of this session you should be able to explain why a fully
connected layer is a poor fit for image- or sequence-like data; explain
convolution as a small, shared, sliding weighted sum, and why weight
sharing gives translation equivariance and (combined with pooling)
invariance; place AlexNet, VGGNet, GoogLeNet, and ResNet on a rough
timeline of the "deep learning era" of computer vision; and describe how
convolutional ideas extend from 2D images to 1D biological sequences and
2D contact maps.

## Why a fully connected layer fails for images (and long sequences)

Every model so far in this course — the perceptron, the softmax
classifier, the flat MLP that classified subcellular localization in
Days 8-9 — treats its input as one long, unstructured vector: every
input position gets its own independent weight, with no notion that
some positions are *near* each other. For a small 150-residue one-hot
sequence (Day 8-9's case study) that's already 3,000 weights per hidden
unit; for a modest $224 \times 224 \times 3$ color image it would be
over 150,000. Two real problems follow. First, **parameter explosion**:
a fully connected layer wastes enormous numbers of weights on
essentially the same task learned independently at every position.
Second, and more fundamentally, **no structural notion of locality or
position-independence**: a cat in the top-left corner of an image and
the same cat shifted to the bottom-right corner look, to a flat
fully-connected layer, like two completely unrelated inputs — every one
of its weights is tied to an absolute position, so nothing it learned
about "cat features here" transfers to "the same features shifted
somewhere else." A convolutional layer fixes both at once with one idea:
use a small kernel, and *slide the same kernel* across every position
instead of learning a separate weight per position.

### Weight sharing gives equivariance, and — with pooling — invariance

A 1D convolution applies the same small kernel at every position of its
input. If the input is shifted, the kernel sees the same local pattern,
just later — so the output feature map shifts by exactly the same
amount. This is **translation equivariance**, and it is a structural
property of weight sharing itself: it holds even for a completely
untrained, randomly-initialized kernel. The notebook demonstrates this
directly — a random 1D kernel applied to a signal, and to the same
signal shifted by 10 positions, produces outputs that agree to floating-
point precision once you account for the shift:

![A random, untrained 1D convolution applied to a signal and to the same signal shifted by 10 positions. The shifted input's output (green) matches the original output shifted by the same amount (orange dashed) almost exactly — equivariance is a property of the shared kernel, not something learned.](figs/day10-conv-equivariance.png){width=90%}

Equivariance alone still leaves the detected feature at a
position-dependent spot in the output. Adding **global pooling** (taking
the max, or the mean, over the whole feature map) removes the remaining
position information: the *value* found is preserved under a shift, so
its maximum is too. Weight-shared convolution (equivariant) followed by
position-independent pooling is exactly what gives a convolutional
network **translation invariance** — verified directly in the notebook,
where the max-pooled output is numerically identical for the original
and the shifted signal.

- 3Blue1Brown, ["But what is a convolution?"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KuXjwB4LzSA) — the general mathematical view of discrete convolution (probability, image processing, FFTs), a level below the CNN-specific weight-sharing/equivariance argument above

## From images to biological data

The same idea generalizes past 2D images. A protein sequence is a 1D
signal over a 20-letter alphabet — exactly the kind of data where a
**1D convolution** (a kernel that slides along the sequence rather than
across a 2D grid) makes sense, for the same reason it makes sense for
images: a short motif (a binding site, a transmembrane segment, a
signal peptide) should be detected the same way regardless of *where*
in the sequence it occurs. Two amino acids' spatial proximity in a
folded structure can likewise be represented as a **contact map** — an
$L \times L$ image-like grid, one pixel per residue pair, where the
value marks whether that pair is in contact in the folded protein — a
natural fit for an ordinary 2D convolution, the same kind used on
photographs.

## Case study: subcellular localization, revisited with a 1D CNN

Days 8-9 built a flat, fully-connected classifier for the same
150-residue, 5-class subcellular-localization dataset used throughout
this section (700 proteins, balanced to 140 per class, one-hot encoded,
490/105/105 train/val/test split — the notebook re-fetches the exact
same data live from UniProt and confirms every one of those counts
matches before continuing). Here, the identical dataset and split feed a
small 1D-CNN instead: two convolutional layers (kernel size 7 — each
filter looks at a 7-residue window at a time) with global average
pooling before a final linear layer to the 5 classes.

That single architectural change has a real, measured effect on model
size: the 1D-CNN has **19,237** trainable parameters, versus the flat
MLP's **192,389** — a 10x reduction, entirely from weight sharing across
positions instead of learning an independent weight for each of the
150 positions.

Trained the same way as Day 9 (Adam, early stopping on validation
accuracy) and evaluated on the identical held-out test set:

| Metric | Day 8: untrained MLP | Day 9: trained MLP | Day 10: trained 1D-CNN |
|---|---|---|---|
| Accuracy | 0.248 | 0.590 | 0.562 |
| Macro F1 | 0.176 | 0.584 | 0.568 |
| MCC | 0.086 | 0.492 | 0.456 |
| Macro AUROC | 0.542 | 0.828 | 0.844 |

Reported honestly, not spun: the 1D-CNN does **not** clearly beat the
flat MLP on raw accuracy/F1/MCC here — it's slightly behind on all
three, though slightly ahead on AUROC. With only 700 short sequences and
a task where the *combination* of many distributed positions (not one
local, translatable motif) may carry most of the signal, weight sharing
doesn't obviously help accuracy on this particular dataset. What it
reliably buys, independent of whether accuracy improves, is the 10x
parameter reduction above — the same predictive signal (if anything,
slightly higher AUROC) from a far smaller number of weights. That
parameter efficiency, not a guaranteed accuracy win, is convolution's
real, general argument — and it becomes decisive on the much longer,
genuinely locally-structured inputs (full-length images, long
sequences) where a flat fully-connected layer would be completely
impractical to fit in memory at all.

## Classic architectures: AlexNet and the 2012 ImageNet moment

Convolutional networks existed well before 2012, but a single result
that year is widely credited with starting the current deep-learning
era: **AlexNet** (Krizhevsky, Sutskever & Hinton, 2012), an 8-layer CNN,
won the ImageNet Large Scale Visual Recognition Challenge with a top-5
error of **15.3%** — more than **10.8 percentage points** ahead of the
runner-up, a margin large enough that it changed what the field
considered worth trying. The years that followed pushed the same
convolution-and-weight-sharing idea deeper and pushed the error down
further:

| Network | Year | Depth | Top-5 error |
|---|---|---|---|
| AlexNet | 2012 | 8 layers | 15.3% |
| VGGNet | 2014 | 16-19 layers | 7.3% |
| GoogLeNet (Inception) | 2014 | 22 layers | 6.7% |
| ResNet | 2015 | up to 152 layers | 3.6% |

(Figures cross-checked against Wikipedia's AlexNet and ResNet pages, not
taken from a single source.) Two ideas made networks this deep trainable
at all, worth knowing by name rather than in full mechanical detail:
**1×1 convolutions** (GoogLeNet/Inception) let a layer cheaply change
its number of channels without touching spatial structure, controlling
parameter growth as networks got wider; and **skip connections**
(ResNet) let a layer's input skip past it unchanged, which is what
finally made stacking over 100 layers trainable at all — before ResNet,
simply adding more layers to a plain CNN made training *harder*, not
better (the "degradation problem"), because gradients had to pass
through every intervening layer just as Day 9's vanishing-gradient
discussion described for a much smaller network.

### Modern practice: transfer learning

Training a network this deep from scratch is expensive (VGG-16's
original training took 2-3 weeks on a single GPU). In practice, almost
nobody does that for a new task: instead, a network pretrained on
ImageNet is reused as a fixed feature extractor, with only a small new
head trained for the new task — **transfer learning**. This is possible
because the early layers of an image classifier tend to learn generic,
reusable features (edges, textures, simple shapes) regardless of what
the network was ultimately trained to classify; only the later layers
are task-specific. `notebooks/ch08.ipynb` demonstrates this pattern
directly with pretrained `torchvision` models (VGG16, GoogLeNet,
ResNet-50) — worth knowing as an idiom even though this course doesn't
run a multi-week ImageNet training itself.

## Case study: protein contact prediction

`notebooks/protein_contact_prediction.ipynb` (in this repository)
demonstrates the 2D-convolution idea from the section above concretely:
a U-Net-style encoder-decoder CNN, with skip connections in the same
spirit as ResNet's, predicting a full $L \times L$ contact map from a
sequence's per-position features — a dense, pixel-to-pixel prediction
task rather than the single-label classification this page's other
case study uses. **Important caveat, stated plainly**: that notebook
trains on synthetic, randomly-generated protein sequences and synthetic
contact labels, not a real experimentally-derived contact dataset — it
demonstrates the architecture and the mechanics, not a claim about real
predictive accuracy. Real systems solving this problem for actual
protein structures (trRosetta, and later AlphaFold2) add multiple
sequence alignments for evolutionary signal and attention mechanisms for
long-range dependencies on top of the same basic convolutional idea.

## The notebook

`notebooks/day10-cnns-in-code.ipynb` has two parts: a from-scratch,
no-training-required demonstration of convolution's translation
equivariance (and, with pooling, invariance) on a random 1D kernel; and
the subcellular-localization case study above, re-fetching Day 8-9's
exact dataset and re-running its exact split, this time through a real
1D-CNN classifier, with every parameter count and metric in the table
above computed and verified there, not asserted. Open it in

yourself.

A light, tool-based exercise: work through
`notebooks/protein_contact_prediction.ipynb`'s synthetic contact-map
case study, then compare its 2D-convolutional U-Net architecture against
Day 10's own 1D-CNN — same underlying idea (weight-shared convolution
plus skip-connection-style architecture choices), applied to a denser,
pixel-to-pixel prediction task instead of single-label classification.

## What's next

Day 11 asks what happens when position isn't fixed-length and local at
all, but sequential and open-ended: RNNs and LSTMs process one position
at a time, carrying a hidden state forward, rather than looking at a
fixed-size local window the way a convolution does.
